# 2 Maccabees Chapter 15 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 15 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_015_page_001.jpg

---

**15:1** When Nicanor learned that Judas and his men were in the region of Samaria, he resolved to attack them with complete safety on the day of rest.

**15:2** The Jews who were compelled to follow him said, "Do not destroy so savagely and barbarously, but show respect for the day that the All-seeing has honored and made holy above all other days."

**15:3** The thrice-accursed wretch asked whether there was a sovereign in heaven who had commanded the observance of the sabbath day.

**15:4** When they replied, "It is the living Lord himself, the sovereign in heaven, who commanded the seventh day to be kept,"

**15:5** he retorted, "And I too am a sovereign on earth, and I command you to take up arms and carry out the king's orders." He did not, however, succeed in carrying out his design.

**15:6** So Nicanor, in his utter arrogance and presumption, had resolved to erect a public monument of his victory over Judas and his men.

**15:7** But Maccabeus never ceased to trust with complete confidence that he would receive help from the Lord.

**15:8** He urged his men not to fear the attack of the Gentiles, but to keep in mind the help they had previously received from heaven, and to expect the victory and aid that would come to them from the Almighty.

**15:9** Encouraging them from the law and the prophets, and reminding them also of the struggles they had already come through successfully, he roused their eagerness.

**15:10** Having stirred their spirits, he gave his orders, at the same time pointing out the treachery of the Gentiles and their disregard of oaths.

**15:11** He armed each of them, not so much with the confidence of shield and spear as with the inspiration of brave words; and he cheered them all by recounting a dream worthy of belief, a kind of waking vision, in the following terms.

**15:12** What he saw was this: Onias, who had been high priest, a noble and good man, of modest bearing, gentle in manner, gracious in speech, and trained from childhood in all things befitting excellence — this man, with his hands outstretched, was praying for the whole Jewish community.

**15:13** Then in the same way there appeared a man of distinguished grey hair and dignity, of marvelous and surpassing majesty.

**15:14** Onias spoke and said, "This is the man who loves the family of Israel and prays much for the people and the holy city — Jeremiah, the prophet of God."

**15:15** Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and delivered to Judas a golden sword, and as he gave it he said:

**15:16** "Take this holy sword, a gift from God, with which you will shatter your adversaries."

**15:17** Encouraged by the words of Judas, so admirable and capable of stirring the soul to valor and fortifying the courage of the young, they determined to attack at once rather than delay, and to decide the issue by a courageous engagement, because the city, the sanctuary, and the holy vessels were in danger.

**15:18** Their concern was not so much for their wives and children or for brothers and relatives — their greatest and first concern was for the consecrated sanctuary.

**15:19** And those who were in the city were in no lesser anguish, being troubled at the prospect of the encounter in the open field.

**15:20** While everyone was now awaiting the coming decision, and the enemy had already drawn near, and the army was drawn up in battle order, with the wild beasts stationed at a favorable position and the cavalry posted on the flanks,

**15:21** Maccabeus, surveying the forces before him — the variety of weapons, the ferocity of the war animals — stretched out his hands toward heaven and called upon the Lord who works wonders, knowing that victory comes not from weapons but that God grants it to whomever he judges worthy.

**15:22** He cried out and said: "You, O Lord, sent your angel in the time of King Hezekiah of Judea and he killed a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp of Sennacherib.

**15:23** So now, O Sovereign of the heavens, send a good angel to go before us, to bring terror and trembling.

**15:24** By the might of your arm let those be struck down who come with blasphemy against your holy people." With these words he ended.

**15:25** Nicanor and his forces advanced with trumpets and battle songs.

**15:26** But Judas and his men met the enemy with invocations and prayers.

**15:27** Fighting with their hands and praying to God in their hearts, they laid low no fewer than thirty-five thousand men and were greatly gladdened by the manifestation of God.

**15:28** When the action was over and they were returning with rejoicing, they recognized Nicanor lying dead in full armor.

**15:29** Then there was shouting and commotion, and they blessed the Sovereign Lord in the language of their ancestors.

**15:30** And the one who had in every way been the chief defender of his fellow citizens — who from his youth had maintained love for his compatriots — ordered that Nicanor's head and arm, cut off at the shoulder, be brought and put on display in Jerusalem.

**15:31** When he arrived there, he called his compatriots together and stationed the priests before the altar; then he sent for those in the citadel

**15:32** and showed them the vile Nicanor's head and that blasphemer's arm, which had been stretched out with such arrogance against the holy house of the Almighty.

**15:33** He also cut out the tongue of the impious Nicanor and said he would give it piecemeal to the birds; he then hung up the visible fruit of his madness opposite the sanctuary.

**15:34** Everyone looked toward heaven and blessed the glorious Lord, saying, "Blessed is he who has kept his own place undefiled."

**15:35** He hung Nicanor's head from the citadel — a clear and conspicuous sign to all of the Lord's help.

**15:36** All decreed by common vote never to let this day go uncelebrated, but to keep the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which in Aramaic is called Adar — the day before Mordecai's day.

**15:37** Thus matters stood with Nicanor, and from that time the city has been in the possession of the Hebrews. And here I will bring my own account to an end.

**15:38** If it is well composed and to the point, that is what I aimed at; if it is poor and mediocre, that was the best I could manage.

**15:39** For just as it is harmful to drink wine by itself or again to drink water by itself, while wine mixed with water is both pleasant and delightful, so the style of a narrative delights the ears of those who read the composition. And with this let it end.
